title: De Lancre's Labourd Campaign: Mass Executions in Basque Country
description: Pierre de Lancre, a Bordeaux judge, conducted a sweeping witch prosecution in the Labourd region of the French Basque Country in 1609 under commission from Henri IV, reportedly burning around 80 people. De Lancre published his account as Tableau de l'Inconstance des Mauvais Anges et Démons (1612), one of the most elaborate descriptions of sabbath proceedings ever written, with detailed accounts of music, dancing, demonic sexuality, and diabolical communion. De Lancre attributed the region's susceptibility to witchcraft partly to the inconstant nature of maritime peoples and the absence of men (at sea) — a remarkable combination of ethnographic observation and misogynist demonology. The Labourd campaign illustrates how royal commission without local judicial oversight could produce rapid large-scale execution.
historiographical_note: L. Roper and other gender historians have analyzed de Lancre's Tableau for its elaborate fantasies of demonic sexuality and female transgression. Gustav Henningsen's work on Spanish Basque witchcraft provides context for the Labourd prosecutions. The campaign was halted partly by protest from the Basque nobility, illustrating that elite opposition could restrain even royally-authorized prosecutions.
source_method: De Lancre, Tableau de l'Inconstance (1612); secondary scholarship on French witchcraft prosecution
